newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO blame each other for Hebron stalemate.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO blame each other for Hebron stalemate.

text.p: The PLO and Israel blamed one another on Tuesday for stalled talks on an Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.

A U.S. official said the sides were still too far apart on implementation of the deal signed by Israel's previous government to warrant the return of U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross to mediate the negotiations.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat met his top negotiators in the West Bank self-rule enclave of Ramallah on Tuesday night.
After the meeting, negotiator Hassan Asfour told Reuters:

"The Palestinian leadership has sent an urgent letter to the Israeli side blaming them fully for delaying talks on the Hebron redeployment and for refusing to respond to frequent calls for meetings since last Thursday."
PLO officials said copies were sent to Washington, Russia, Arab states and the European Union.
Israeli spokesman Moshe Fogel denied Israel was refusing to hold talks. He accused Asfour of "repeated lies".

"We're not refusing to hold meetings. The Palestinian delegation has to understand that disinformation...is not going to lead to progress...It's about time that instead of making public statements we sit down and sign the agreement."
Fogel added: "Hassan Asfour has repeated lies in the media including claims in the earlier stages of the talks that there was no progress when indeed progress had been made."
The U.S. Consul General in East Jerusalem, Edward Abbington, met Arafat twice on Tuesday. PLO officials said Arafat rejected ideas not within the agreement. They did not elaborate.

Israel television said Washington presented proposals to bridge the sides' differences on security arrangements. Arafat spokesman Nabil Abu Rdainah denied the report. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's spokesman refused to comment.

Abbington told Reuters in Ramallah: "Ross said a week ago he would return after consultations with the secretary of state and after consultations with the parties when they near an agreement. I don't think we are at the point yet."
He refused to comment on the Israeli television report.
Ross left the region on October 29 after failing to broker a deal in three weeks of talks.

Netanyahu ousted Israel's previous centre-left government in May elections. Palestinians accuse him of trying to change the signed deal. He says he wants more security for some 400 Jews who live and study in Hebron among 100,000 Palestinians.
Netanyahu told Israel television on Tuesday that if Arafat was waiting until U.S. elections ended to move on a deal in hopes of U.S. pressure, he would be disappointed. He added:
"The whole idea that Netanyahu will stand and be whipped by the next president of the United States is simply not serious."
Earlier on Tuesday, Palestinian negotiator, Yasser Abed Rabbo, described negotiations as a "mockery" and called for the talks to be halted.

The recent talks were arranged at a Washington summit after 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed in gunbattles in September, spurred by Israel opening a second entrance to a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem.
Abed Rabbo called for a summit to re-emphasise the land- for-peace foundation of the peace process begun in 1991.

Netanyahu opposes the principle of returning occupied Arab land in return for recognition and peace. Israel has occupied the West Bank and Gaza Strip since 1967 and it handed Gaza and parts of the West Bank to Palestinian rule in 1994 and 1995.

"Without this (formula), there will be an explosion because our differences with Israel are not over redeployment from a few streets in a Palestinian city. They are over the basis of the peace process and the signed agreements," Rabbo said.
